newsitem.title: USA: Maine electric deregulation bill signed.
newsitem.headline: Maine electric deregulation bill signed.

text.p: Gov. Angus King Thursday signed legislation deregulating Maine's electric market, but he warned consumers not to expect to see rate reductions too quickly.
The bill allows an estimated 640,000 consumers to choose between competing power suppliers by March 1, 2000, and requires two utilities to divest their generating assets.
"It is not a panacea but I believe this is the best bill in the country on this subject," said King, who has repeatedly complained Maine's high electric rates are hampering economic development.

King said consumers should not expect immediate rate reductions, "but the expectation and historical evidence tells us that we will see lower electrical rates...in the forseeable future and the rest of the time that we're citizens here in Maine."

Maine's two largest utilities, Central Maine Power and Bangor Hydro, are required to divest their power generating assets. They will be primarily distribution companies but will have limited rights to market power.

Maine Public Service can keep its generating plants because its northern Maine distribution system works as part of the Canadian -- rather than U.S. -- power grid. MPS will have to allow competition in its service area.

Lawmakers have put off until next year a decision on how to compensate utilities for their "stranded costs." CMP has proposed Maine use a securitization plan similar to that enacted by Pennsylvania and several other states.

The utilities have indicated they will ask lawmakers to eliminate a provision limiting transmission companies from selling power to more than 30 percent of the customers within their distribution area.

Utilities Committee co-chair Rep. Kyle Jones said Thursday some lawmakers wanted to bar CMP and Bangor Hydro from doing any power marketing, and he believes the final plan will allow them "to not only survive but to thrive."
